content: The Last Common Ancestor (LCA) refers to the most recent shared ancestor of two populations that diverged due to the formation of a species barrier. LCA of Two Species The evolutionary distance between two species determines how ancient their LCA is. For instance, the LCA of an elephant and an earthworm existed approximately two billion years ago. In contrast, the LCA of an elephant and a Tyrannosaurus rex lived around 300 million years ago. Meanwhile, the LCA of the elephant and the mammoth, two closely related species, existed only about seven million years ago. Other Common Ancestor Terminology The Last Universal Ancestor (LUA) or Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA) refers to a hypothetical unicellular organism that is believed to have given rise to all life on Earth approximately three to four billion years ago. This concept remains a subject of scientific debate. Mitochondrial Eve: Genetic studies have traced human mitochondrial DNA to a single woman, often referred to as Mitochondrial Eve. She is the matrilineal most recent common ancestor of all humans alive today and is estimated to have lived around 150,000 years ago. Y-chromosomal Adam: Similarly, genetic studies have shown that all Y chromosomes in men alive today can be traced back to a single man, known as Y-chromosomal Adam. He is the patrilineal most recent common ancestor and is estimated to have lived approximately 60,000 years ago. Concestor: Richard Dawkins introduced the term concestor as a potential alternative to Last Common Ancestor. Common Ancestor: Any two species share numerous common ancestors throughout their evolutionary history. For example, the ancestors of the elephant and the mammoth were shared for billions of years until their evolutionary paths diverged about seven million years ago, marking the point of their last common ancestor. The term common ancestor is often used in a lineage-specific context, which differs from the species-level context discussed here. In human terms, you and your cousin share a common grandfather. You and your second cousins share a great-grandfather, while you and your sixth cousins may share a great-great-great-great-great-grandfather. It has been estimated that Genghis Khan is a common ancestor to approximately 16 million men alive today. Most Recent Common Ancestor Until 1999, the terms Last and Most Recent Common Ancestor were used interchangeably. However, subsequent research (e.g., by Rohde, Olson, and Chang) has refined the term Most Recent Common Ancestor (MRCA) to refer to a specific ancestor within a species, such as a shared grandparent, rather than the founder of the species itself. Computer simulations suggest that all living humans today could share a common ancestor who lived as recently as 2,000 to 3,000 years ago. This individual, whose identity is lost to history, has been designated the MRCA of all humankind.
